header: Date: 2027-05-18 15:00 PDT; Duration: 48m; Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marcus Hale (Ember CTO), Leah Ortiz (SRE), Jordan Lin (Head of ML). Purpose: discovery on per-token economics, deployment mode tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated vs private), batching/caching levers, and pilot scope.
summary: Ember Payments is evaluating Redwood for an LLM inference path to power transaction risk explanations and internal summaries. Key concerns: per-token costs at scale, latency SLO during peak billing windows, and data residency/SOC2 for payments data. They are leaning toward starting with hosted for speed but want a path to dedicated/private if unit economics or compliance require it.
topics: batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization levers
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for carving out time, quick intro we are Redwood, I am Alex AE, and Priya SE. how are you all?
[00:04] Marcus Hale: good thanks, Marcus here. quick context we run Ember Payments, we do transaction monitoring and want to add explanatory text on chargebacks and merchant disputes. main ask is cost predictability and low latency for support flows.
[00:15] Alex Chen: great, and Priya follow me on technical questions. first high level, can you share current qps and typical prompt lengths?
[00:22] Jordan Lin: yeah so production currently is about 250 rps at peak for internal tooling, customer-facing support flows maybe 40 rps. prompt lengths vary, average 600 tokens in, 150 tokens out, but some long summaries hit 2k tokens out.
[00:36] Priya Kapoor: okay that mix matters a lot for batching and caching. are you using persistent KV cache today?
[00:40] Leah Ortiz: no live caching, just a microcache at edge for user sessions, nothing model-specific.
[00:45] Alex Chen: perfect, so from Redwood's side two levers reduce per-token cost: batching (amortize compute across requests) and KV/prefix caching (skip repeated prefix compute). we also have quantized model variants to reduce GPU memory and cost.
[00:58] Marcus Hale: enums question — if we go hosted and then later need dedicated, how smooth is migration? what's the unit-econ delta you typically see?
[01:06] Priya Kapoor: migration is generally straightforward via model pinning and routing policies. unit-econ delta depends on load shape. for steady high throughput dedicated often reduces per-token by 20-40% relative to hosted list price because of reserved capacity and better batch packing; for spiky workloads hosted can be cheaper because you avoid reserved commit.
[01:23] Jordan Lin: that 20-40% range, is that for same quantization level?
[01:27] Priya Kapoor: yes same quantization; if you move to int8 or q4 variants you get additional 10-25% improvements but must validate quality.
[01:34] Marcus Hale: latency tradeoffs? our SLAs are 300ms p95 for support chat, longer for async summarization.
[01:40] Priya Kapoor: batching helps throughput but increases tail latency if you set large batch windows. Redwood supports continuous batching with latency buckets so you can set SLO targets — e.g., keep a 50ms batching window for low-latency flows and a 200ms window for background summarization. KV cache cuts cold-start tokens so highly repetitive prefixes are near-instant.
[01:56] Leah Ortiz: are KV caches persisted across model versions and restarts? we need deterministic behavior for reconciles.
[02:01] Priya Kapoor: yes, we persist cache entries and provide TTL controls; when you rollout model versions you can configure cache warming or invalidation. there are edge cases where model architecture change invalidates cache, we handle that via invalidation flags in rollout config.
[02:17] Marcus Hale: on security — payments data, PCI scope. do you have an isolated offering?
[02:22] Alex Chen: Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) is for high-regulated customers; Dedicated can be VPC-connected with customer-managed keys and audit logs. we are SOC2 Type II and can provide ATO artifacts.
[02:33] Leah Ortiz: KMS — can you integrate with our AWS KMS and HSM for key wrapping?
[02:37] Priya Kapoor: yes we support customer-managed KMS with HSM-backed keys and envelope encryption. audit logs are per-request and can be exported to your SIEM.
[02:44] Jordan Lin: pricing discussion — what's the hosted rate per-token and how do you handle embeddings vs generation?
[02:49] Alex Chen: we price hosted generation per 1k tokens, and embeddings separately per 1k units. I'll send exact sheet, but ballpark: hosted generation for a 7B-class model is $0.80–$1.20 per 1k tokens depending on model; embeddings are lower. Dedicated pricing converts to reserved GPU pool with committed spend and lower per-token rate, we can work through an example calc.
[03:09] Marcus Hale: that's helpful. can you walk through an exemplar unit-econ calc?
[03:13] Priya Kapoor: sure — assume 10k requests/day, avg 750 tokens in, 150 tokens out = 9M tokens/day. at $1/1k tokens that's $9k/day or ~$270k/mo. with dedicated and batching improvements plus q4 quant you'd likely land around $160k–$200k/mo. but these are noisy numbers; we should run your actual prompt distribution through our bench.
[03:35] Marcus Hale: those numbers are big, need to validate, and also figure out cost vs latency for our 300ms SLO.
[03:41] Alex Chen: understood. pilot is the fastest path — we do a 30-day pilot with your workload, run both hosted and dedicated-config benchmarks and measure token costs, p95 latency, cost per 1M tokens, and cache hit rates.
[03:52] Marcus Hale: timeline: we want pilot in June if possible, exec sponsor is VP Ops, procurement involved.
[03:57] Alex Chen: good, we'll aim for late June kickoff.
[03:59] [04:00] Priya Kapoor: technical detail — for your 2k-token out summaries we recommend splitting into chunked generation with caching for sections that repeat across summaries; that reduces average generated tokens. also suggest using reranking only for top-k where needed to avoid per-token inflation.
[04:18] Jordan Lin: chunking approach — would that change the prompt distribution and increase request count?
[04:23] Priya Kapoor: yes it increases requests but each request is smaller and you can batch them together to reuse KV cache; overall compute and tokens can be lower. it's a workload engineering tradeoff.
[04:35] Leah Ortiz: what's Redwood's recommendation for autoscaling if we go dedicated? spikes during settlement windows can be 4-5x baseline for a few hours.
[04:44] Priya Kapoor: Dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscale policies. you can configure guaranteed baseline nodes and burst pools with cold-start thresholds; for long tail spikes we recommend capacity reservation plus fallback routing to hosted to avoid dropped requests.
[04:58] Marcus Hale: fallback to hosted — does that affect data residency? we cannot send raw transactions outside region.
[05:03] Alex Chen: good point — fallback routing can be region-aware. for cross-env fallback we'd only route to compatible private/dedicated instances in approved regions; we can exclude hosted fallback if that violates residency.
[05:14] Jordan Lin: procurement and cost — if we commit to dedicated, what's minimum term?
[05:18] Alex Chen: standard term options are monthly or annual commitments; discounts grow with term and committed spend. we can build a blended plan for the pilot to test economics without a large commit.
[05:27] Marcus Hale: do you have hard numbers for cache hit improvement we should expect?
[05:30] Priya Kapoor: depends on prefix repetition; for transactional systems with templated language we often see 40–70% effective token savings for shared prefixes after warmup. but again depends on how much of the prompt is unique per request.
[05:45] Leah Ortiz: is there any observability where we can see token-level breakdown and which tokens are from cache vs compute?
[05:49] Alex Chen: yes Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdown and cache hit rates, per-route latency, and cost attribution. we'll grant a demo account and a tokenized sample dashboard during pilot.
[06:01] Marcus Hale: security docs — can you send SOC2 and network topology for private option?
[06:06] Alex Chen: yes, will include SOC2 and sample network diagram in the security packet.
[06:10] Jordan Lin: for the pilot, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[06:14] Priya Kapoor: sample prompt traces, SLOs, a representative traffic generator (we'll provide), and a few sample long-summary prompts. also access to a staging dataset for quality checks.
[06:25] Marcus Hale: we can provide that. what about rate limiting and quotas?
[06:29] Alex Chen: Redwood supports per-token quotas, per-route rate limits, and token-based billing ceilings with alerts. you can set per-token budgets to avoid runaway spend.
[06:38] Leah Ortiz: one more — audit logs retention, we may need 7 years for some records.
[06:43] Alex Chen: we support configurable retention; longer retention is an enterprise add-on. we'll note retention requirements in the security packet.
[06:51] Jordan Lin: any hidden costs — data egress, model switching, or re-quantization rework?
[06:56] Priya Kapoor: main items to plan: storage for persisted KV caches (small), network for model downloads (one-time), and engineering time for prompt engineering/quality checks. model switching and quantization testing are part of onboarding and scoped in pilot estimate. no surprise per-token surcharge beyond the listed rates.
[07:11] Marcus Hale: can we see a sample forecast: for 10k req/day and 9M tokens/day you estimated 270k/mo hosted and 160–200k/mo dedicated. show calculations in the sheet please.
[07:20] Alex Chen: will do. we'll include sensitivity to batching latency windows and cache hit rates.
[07:24] [07:30] Priya Kapoor: operational note — for critical low-latency flows you may prefer an edge-insulated dedicated pool with strict batching windows and small batch sizes, and accept higher cost per token; for background summarization you can push to batch-heavy nodes with aggressive quantization.
[07:44] Marcus Hale: that split sounds reasonable. internal decision will be cost-driven for customer-facing flows and lower-cost for backfill.
[07:51] Leah Ortiz: who will be our Redwood SE contact during pilot?
[07:54] Alex Chen: Priya is primary and we'll loop an onboarding engineer once pilot is signed.
[07:59] Jordan Lin: timeline recap?
[08:01] Alex Chen: we will send price sheet by 5/20, benchmark runbook by 5/21, you confirm pilot scope by 5/25, pilot kickoff last week of June.
[08:10] Marcus Hale: sounds good. thanks all.
[08:12] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and files.
[48:00] [call end]
